name: Spatial text rendering and ASCII layout comprehension. A cluster rather than one artifact. Named methods and evaluations: Spatial Text Rendering (STR), the document-to-text-skeleton method published by Abwab.ai for feeding visually complex documents to text-only LLMs; Learning to Draw ASCII Improves Spatial Reasoning in Language Models (arXiv:2604.14641) with its Text2Space dataset; ASCIIBench (arXiv:2512.04125); ASCIIEval / Visual Perception in Text Strings (arXiv:2410.01733) and the Vision-in-Text Challenge (ViTC); Large Language Models Understand Layout (arXiv:2407.05750); A Simple yet Effective Layout Token in LLMs for Document Understanding (arXiv:2503.18434); Visualization-of-Thought (arXiv:2404.03622); Stuck in the Matrix: Probing Spatial Reasoning in LLMs (arXiv:2510.20198); Table Meets LLM (arXiv:2305.13062) for the table-serialisation-format comparison. Adjacent practice: box-drawing-character diagrams, whitespace-preserved PDF text layers, and the long tradition of terminal UI rendering.
kind: Research results plus one published industrial method (STR) and several benchmarks. Not a standard, not a browser feature, not a service. For this project it is the literature that governs whether the ASCII cartesian wireframe is a good idea and how it should be shaped.
maturity: Research-stage and fast-moving, with a small amount of industrial practice. STR is a described production method for a specific document-understanding use case rather than a released library. The benchmarks (ASCIIBench, ASCIIEval, Text2Space) all date from 2024-2026 and are not yet standard. The one durable, well-replicated finding is the read/write asymmetry described below; almost everything else in the area is single-paper. Nothing here should be treated as settled, and the design implications drawn below are the robust ones.
license: The papers are arXiv preprints, freely citable. Text2Space, ASCIIBench and ASCIIEval are released research datasets, typically under permissive or research-use terms. STR is described in a company engineering write-up with no code release located, so it is a method to reimplement rather than adopt. Box-drawing characters are Unicode and unencumbered. Nothing blocks use here. [uncertain] on the specific dataset licences and on whether any STR reference implementation exists.
keeps_and_discards: The whole family converts SPATIAL relations into CHARACTER-GRID positions, keeping relative position, alignment, containment and adjacency, and discarding exact metrics -- pixel coordinates, font sizes, colours, precise widths. STR specifically extracts and preserves a document's structural SKELETON: it renders the document into a text grid using box-drawing characters and whitespace so that the arrangement that gives a form or a financial statement its meaning survives into something a text-only model can read, then downscales so the grid fits a token budget. The characteristic loss is quantisation: two things that are 3 pixels apart and two things that are 30 pixels apart may land in the same or adjacent cells depending on the downscale factor, so fine alignment distinctions are destroyed while gross layout survives. For this project the important framing is that an ASCII wireframe is a LOSSY PROJECTION OF GEOMETRY, not a representation of the DOM -- it answers 'what is next to what' and cannot answer 'what does this say' beyond whatever labels are placed in the cells. It is a complement to the fold, never a substitute.
structure_preserved: Two-dimensional adjacency and containment, expressed positionally rather than by nesting. That is a genuinely different structural vocabulary from a tree: a wireframe naturally expresses 'this block is to the right of that one' and 'this is inside that box', which a DOM tree expresses only indirectly, and it naturally destroys 'this is the third child of that element', which the tree expresses exactly. Reading order is implied by scan order (left-to-right, top-to-bottom) rather than declared, which is an assumption that fails for multi-column layouts and for RTL content. Tabular relations survive well -- a grid is the native case, and this is why the technique is used for financial documents and forms. Shadow boundaries have no expression at all. The design consequence is that a wireframe and a trie carry complementary and non-overlapping structural information, and the join between them must be explicit: each cell or box in the wireframe should carry the address of the node it renders, or the two representations cannot be reconciled by the model or by anything else.
interactive_elements: Nothing intrinsic; controls appear only if the renderer draws them. The practical pattern in terminal-UI-style rendering is to mark controls with distinguishing glyphs ([ ] for a checkbox, ( ) for a radio, [Button] for a button, ___ for a field) which is compact, conventional and readable, and which restores affordance information that a pure box diagram loses. This is the natural place for the actuator layer's affordance display, because it locates the control on screen -- which is exactly what an actuator needs and what the fold deliberately does not carry.
interactive_state_fidelity: Available cheaply and conventionally if the renderer chooses to encode it: [x] versus [ ], (o) versus ( ), a greyed or bracketed label for disabled, a highlight glyph for focus. The cost is a character or two per control, which is far cheaper than any prose encoding. The caution is that these conventions are implicit and unlabelled, so a model must infer them; the evidence below on read/write asymmetry suggests models READ such conventions reasonably well, but no study measures comprehension of state glyphs specifically. Where state matters more than position, prose or an attribute annotation in the fold is the more reliable channel and the wireframe should be treated as a locator rather than as the state record.
layout_awareness: Total and by definition -- this is a geometry-consuming representation and there is no version of it that is not. That makes the constraint verdict trivial and important: an ASCII wireframe is ACTUATOR-LAYER ONLY, exactly as the project already specifies, and the value of this item is in confirming that placement and in saying how to build the thing once it is there. The geometry it consumes is coarse -- bounding boxes and a downscale factor, not full computed style -- so the peripheral it reads from can be a small per-address record (x, y, width, height, visible) rather than anything richer, which keeps the geometry peripheral genuinely peripheral.
javascript_required: Geometry must come from a rendered page, so yes in practice: bounding boxes require layout, and reading them (getBoundingClientRect or equivalent) forces style and layout resolution. This is a real cost distinct from the fold's -- the fold can be produced without touching layout, and the wireframe cannot, so the two have different performance and different observability profiles. Forcing layout is also, unlike a serialisation read, potentially perceptible to a page through timing, which is a further argument for keeping wireframe generation on the actuator path and out of the routine read path.
evaluation_method: Three distinguishable methods across the cluster. (1) COMPREHENSION benchmarks: present an ASCII or spatially-rendered artifact and ask questions about it, scoring accuracy -- ASCIIEval/ViTC does this for ASCII art recognition, ASCIIBench for classification and generation of ASCII images, and the layout-understanding papers for document QA. (2) CONSTRUCTION benchmarks: give a natural-language spatial description and require the model to emit a correct ASCII grid, scored against ground truth -- Text2Space's contribution, and the methodologically important one because it separates failures in BUILDING a spatial representation from failures in REASONING over one, which every earlier study conflated. (3) DOWNSTREAM task evaluation: does feeding a spatially-rendered document to a text-only model beat the alternatives (OCR text without layout, a vision-language model on the image), which is STR's framing. The first two are well controlled with synthetic ground truth; the third is the one that matters for a deployment decision and is the least rigorously reported.
corpus_size_and_origins: Text2Space comprises 20,000 instances with a 1,000-sample test split, generated from connected spatial graphs with two to eight components and one to twelve directional relations, so it is fully synthetic with exact ground truth and controlled difficulty -- excellent internal validity, no real-document content at all. ASCIIBench is a filtered dataset of 5,315 class-labelled ASCII images, drawn from existing ASCII art collections. ASCIIEval/ViTC uses ASCII art rendering of characters and objects. STR's evaluation is on financial and form-like documents in a business setting, and the write-up indicates work on Arabic-script documents, which would make it one of the very few sources in this whole research set with genuine RTL coverage -- worth verifying directly rather than relying on this summary. Nothing in the cluster evaluates on web page layouts specifically, and no benchmark uses a rendered browser viewport as its spatial substrate, so transfer to a page wireframe is by analogy. [uncertain] on STR's exact corpus, language coverage and reported figures -- the primary write-up was not retrievable during this research (403), so its details here are second-hand from search summaries and should be confirmed before citing.
reported_precision_recall: The strong, directly usable numbers come from Text2Space and they are the most decision-relevant in this item. READ/WRITE ASYMMETRY: across tested models, comprehension of ASCII layouts substantially exceeds construction of them, with a construction gap of 13 to 27 percentage points; GPT-4.1 scored 72.5% on interpreting ASCII grids versus 53.6% on constructing them, and gpt-oss-20B -- a reasoning model with robust interpretation -- failed construction 56% of the time. Denominator is the 1,000-instance Text2Space test split. Models evaluated: Llama-3-70B-Instruct, Qwen 2.5-7B through Qwen3-235B-A22B, GPT-4.1, gpt-oss-20B. TRANSFER RESULT: fine-tuning Qwen3-30B-A3B (LoRA) on layout CONSTRUCTION improved text-only spatial reasoning by over 7 percentage points, and the gains transferred to three external benchmarks (StepGame, bAbI Task 19, SpartQA) -- so the ability to build a spatial representation is a transferable skill, not a formatting trick. GENERAL LIMITATION, from the ASCII-art line: models remain far behind humans on transformation tasks (translation, rotation, robustness to noise) and on shape recognition from character grids. TABLE FORMAT: the table-serialisation literature compares CSV, JSON, XML, markdown, HTML and spreadsheet formats for table reasoning and finds format materially affects accuracy, but the reported orderings are task- and model-dependent and no single format wins across the board -- so 'use markdown tables' is not an evidence-backed default. NOT LOCATED: any measurement of ASCII wireframe comprehension for WEB PAGE layouts specifically, or of how wireframe fidelity trades against token cost.
independent_oracle: Strong for the synthetic benchmarks: Text2Space's ground-truth grids are generated from spatial graphs, so correctness is exactly decidable and shares nothing with the model. ASCIIBench's class labels are external. The comprehension side has an unusual and valuable property -- because a grid is structurally verifiable, a claimed spatial relation can be checked mechanically against the grid, which makes ASCII a good probe medium precisely because it is machine-checkable while remaining in token space; the Text2Space authors make this argument explicitly and it is correct. What has NO oracle is the downstream question: whether a wireframe of a real page conveys the layout accurately, which would require human judgement or a task with a spatial ground truth, and no such evaluation exists for web pages.
evidence_independence: Mostly academic and independent. Text2Space's numbers are its authors' but are measured on third-party models including two they did not train, and the transfer result to three EXTERNAL benchmarks is the kind of corroboration that raises confidence materially. ASCIIBench and ASCIIEval are academic benchmark papers. The one vendor-shaped source is STR, published by a company applying it commercially to document understanding, whose write-up naturally argues that its method beats the alternatives; no independent replication was located, and its figures should be treated as vendor-reported until verified. Note also that the table-format comparisons circulate heavily through vendor and practitioner blogs with mutually contradictory conclusions -- the HTML-versus-markdown-for-agents genre in particular is almost entirely vendor-authored and should not be cited as evidence in either direction.
page_archetype_coverage: Unmeasured for web pages, and mechanically the spread should be large. Wireframes should be most informative for archetypes where position carries meaning that structure does not: forms and service flows (field-to-label association, grouping, tab order implied by position), dashboards, tabular product comparisons, and multi-column layouts. They should be nearly worthless for prose archetypes -- an article or documentation page is a single column of text and its wireframe is a box, conveying nothing the tree does not. Listing and collection pages are intermediate: the grid arrangement of cards is real information, but it is highly repetitive and compresses to 'a grid of N similar boxes', which is one line of prose. That reasoning suggests wireframe generation should be conditional rather than routine -- worth its cost on some archetypes and pure overhead on others -- but conditioning on archetype would itself be a structural classifier, so the conditioning must be on a mechanical signal (column count, aspect-ratio variance of sibling boxes) or on explicit operator request.
script_and_locale_behaviour: The sharpest practical problem in this item and the one most likely to be overlooked. An ASCII grid assumes MONOSPACE character cells, and that assumption breaks in several ways for non-Latin content. East Asian characters are typically double-width, so a grid aligned by character count is misaligned by half a cell per CJK character unless the renderer accounts for East Asian Width -- a well-known terminal problem with a well-known solution (wcwidth-style width tables) that must be implemented deliberately. Combining marks occupy zero width and inflate character counts without inflating display width. RTL text inside an LTR grid is the worst case: the bidirectional algorithm reorders characters for display, so a naive grid containing Arabic or Hebrew labels renders with the text running the wrong way relative to the box that contains it, and worse, the CHARACTER SEQUENCE the model receives is in logical order while the visual arrangement the grid encodes is in display order -- the two disagree, and there is no representation that satisfies both. Emoji and other wide symbols have the same width problem as CJK. If the project's wireframe is to be script-invariant it must compute cell widths by display width rather than by code point count, and must decide explicitly and document how RTL labels are placed. STR's reported work on Arabic documents is therefore the most interesting part of that method and the part worth investigating first. Note finally that the model's own tokeniser sees the grid as tokens, and whitespace runs tokenise differently across tokenisers, so grid alignment costs a variable number of tokens depending on the padding character used.
leaks_outward: Nothing to a page from the rendering itself. Two indirect points. Producing the wireframe requires reading geometry, which forces layout -- a computational side effect a page could in principle time, unlike a pure serialisation read. And a wireframe of a rendered viewport captures WHAT WAS ON SCREEN, so on an authenticated page it discloses the visible arrangement including anything incidentally present, in the same way a screenshot does but at much lower resolution; it is a coarse screenshot in text, and should be treated with a screenshot's privacy posture rather than a serialisation's.
mechanism_detectability: Low but non-zero, and higher than the fold's. The geometry reads that a wireframe needs (getBoundingClientRect, offsetWidth, or a CDP layout-metrics call) force synchronous layout, which is a measurable performance event; a page instrumenting long tasks or rAF jitter could in principle observe repeated forced reflows, and a page that mutates and then measures can amplify the signal. This is a genuine detectability differential between the fold (no layout, undetectable) and the wireframe (forces layout, faintly detectable), and it is another reason to generate wireframes on demand for actuation rather than continuously.
countermeasures: Batch geometry reads to avoid layout thrashing (read all rectangles, then write, never interleave), which both reduces cost and flattens the timing signature; generate wireframes only when an actuator needs one; use IntersectionObserver or a cached layout snapshot rather than repeated synchronous measurement where possible. Against fidelity failure, the countermeasure is to carry addresses in the wireframe so any cell can be cross-checked against the fold.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not measured for web wireframes anywhere. The measurable quantity, and the experiment worth running: render a page's viewport as an ASCII wireframe at several downscale factors, then ask a fixed set of mechanically-checkable spatial questions (is A above B, is C inside D, are E and F in the same row) whose ground truth comes from the raw bounding boxes, and plot accuracy against grid size and token cost. Ground truth is exact and free because it comes from the same geometry the wireframe was built from, so this is an oracle-free evaluation in the same sense Text2Space's is. That curve would directly determine the wireframe's default resolution and nobody has produced it.
gate_state_at_capture: Not represented, but a wireframe is unusually good at REVEALING it: a consent overlay, paywall interstitial or modal login is a large box occupying the centre of the viewport, and that is exactly the kind of gross layout fact a wireframe conveys well and a DOM tree conveys poorly. So a wireframe is a cheap gate-state INDICATOR even though it is not a gate-state record -- which is a genuine argument for generating one at capture time and storing it alongside the capture, as a compact visual-state witness. Detecting the overlay from the wireframe would be a structural heuristic and is out of bounds; storing the wireframe so a human or an out-of-band process can see the gate is not.
determinism: Deterministic given fixed geometry and a fixed downscale factor -- the rendering is a pure function of a set of rectangles. The geometry itself is not deterministic across loads: viewport size, font availability and fallback, image loading, animation phase, scroll position and lazy content all change the boxes, so the same page produces different wireframes on different loads and on different machines. That instability is inherent to geometry and is a strong reason the wireframe must not be part of the stored canonical artifact -- it is a derived view, regenerable from stored geometry if the geometry is stored, and meaningless if it is not.
determinism_across_versions: Drifts substantially. Layout changes with browser version, font rendering and metrics change with OS and font updates, and device pixel ratio changes with hardware -- all of which shift bounding boxes and therefore the grid. A wireframe is thus pinned to a (browser build, OS, fonts, viewport size, DPR) tuple far more tightly than any DOM-derived artifact, and cross-environment comparison of wireframes is unsound without recording all of it. If wireframes are ever stored, that tuple is mandatory metadata.
reproducibility: Reproducible from stored GEOMETRY, not from a URL. The practical recommendation follows the same shape as everywhere else in this research set: store the per-address bounding-box table as the frozen artifact (it is small -- four numbers and a visibility flag per node) and treat the wireframe as a re-derivable rendering of it at any resolution. That makes the resolution a query parameter rather than a capture decision, allows the downscale-versus-accuracy curve above to be measured offline, and keeps the geometry peripheral genuinely peripheral: a side table keyed by the same address the trie uses, exactly as the project's design specifies.
failure_modes: (1) QUANTISATION COLLAPSE -- at coarse grid resolutions distinct elements merge into one cell and adjacency relations become wrong, not merely imprecise. (2) OVERLAP AND Z-ORDER -- a character grid is 2D with no depth, so overlapping elements, modals over content, sticky headers and absolutely-positioned overlays cannot be represented faithfully; something must win each cell and the loser vanishes silently. (3) OFF-VIEWPORT CONTENT -- a wireframe of the viewport omits everything scrolled out of view, and a wireframe of the full document at viewport resolution is enormous; neither choice is right and both fail quietly. (4) WIDTH MISCALCULATION for CJK, combining marks and emoji, producing a grid that is misaligned in a way that is invisible in the source and obvious in the render. (5) RTL DISORDER, where logical and display order disagree irreconcilably. (6) SCALE MISMATCH -- a page with one enormous element and many tiny ones has no single downscale factor that renders both usefully. (7) CONSTRUCTION FAILURE IF THE MODEL IS ASKED TO WRITE ONE -- the 13-27 point construction gap means a model asked to produce or edit a wireframe will often produce a wrong one, and the error will propagate silently into downstream reasoning. (8) LABEL TRUNCATION -- text placed in a cell must be clipped to fit, and clipping changes meaning.
failure_visibility: Mostly silent, with one useful exception. Quantisation, overlap loss and off-viewport omission all produce a plausible-looking grid with no indication that anything was lost. Width miscalculation is the exception: a misaligned grid usually LOOKS misaligned, which is a rare case of a fidelity failure that announces itself. The fixes for the silent cases are cheap and should be mandatory: report the downscale factor and the resulting cell size in the rendering's header; mark cells where more than one element competed with an overlap glyph and a count; state explicitly what fraction of the document is outside the rendered region; and mark truncated labels with an ellipsis rather than silently clipping. Every one of these is one character or one header line and each converts an invisible loss into a declared one.
scale_limits: Cost is O(cells) in tokens, and cells grow as the product of grid width and height, so token cost is QUADRATIC in linear resolution -- doubling the fidelity of a wireframe quadruples its cost. That is the single most important cost fact about this representation and it bounds useful resolutions hard: an 80x24 grid is about 2,000 characters before any content, and a 200x60 grid is 12,000. Given the budget analysis in item 30 -- a per-emission budget on the order of 1,500 tokens for a small model in a multi-step session -- a wireframe of any useful resolution consumes an entire emission budget on its own. That is a decisive practical constraint: a wireframe cannot be routine, must be requested, and must be coarse. Geometry collection is separately O(nodes) and forces layout once if batched, or once per read if not.
delta_cost_model: Poor, and this is the representation's worst structural property. Layout is GLOBAL: a single DOM change can reflow the entire document, moving every box, so a delta of one node produces a delta of every cell in the wireframe. There is no bounded per-change cost for a layout-derived rendering, and this is not an implementation deficiency but a property of how layout works. Named exclusions if an incremental wireframe were attempted: (1) reflow, where one insertion moves everything after it and in flex or grid containers everything around it; (2) CSS-driven layout change with no DOM mutation at all -- a media-query or container-query response, a transition, a class change resolving differently -- which produces a completely different wireframe with an empty mutation record, and is the same soundness hole item 24 catalogues, in its most severe form; (3) scroll, which changes the viewport-relative geometry of every element without changing anything else; (4) font loading, which reflows the page asynchronously after initial render; (5) image and media loading, likewise; (6) the quadratic cost of the rendering itself, which must be paid in full for any change since a grid cannot be patched incrementally in a way a model can consume. The correct conclusion, and it aligns exactly with the project's stated architecture, is that geometry is a PERIPHERAL that is re-read on demand and never maintained incrementally, and that any O(delta) claim covers the fold and explicitly excludes the wireframe.
reanchoring_stability: A wireframe has no durable identity of its own -- cells are positions, and positions change. Its stability comes entirely from the addresses attached to it, which is the argument for making every rendered box carry its node address as part of the rendering (or in an accompanying legend keyed by cell). With addresses attached, a wireframe becomes a spatial VIEW over the trie and inherits the trie's re-anchoring properties; without them it is an orphan artifact that cannot be related to anything else and cannot be validated. This should be treated as a hard requirement rather than an enhancement.
adversarial_exposure: Here the wireframe is a genuine asset and it is the most interesting safety finding in this item. Because it is built from GEOMETRY, a wireframe sees exactly what the fold cannot: an element with zero size, positioned off-canvas, or with no painted area simply has no box worth drawing, and an element rendered under another has its cell taken. That means the geometry peripheral is precisely the instrument that can adjudicate the rendering-based concealment class -- the roughly 58.6% of concealed injections using display:none, zero size or off-screen positioning -- which a layout-blind fold structurally cannot see. The design implication is important and specific: the project does not need to put layout in the fold to defend against rendering-based concealment; it needs a CONCEALMENT CHECK IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER that compares the set of addresses present in the fold against the set of addresses with a non-degenerate rendered box, and flags the difference. That check consumes geometry, lives on the actuator side, respects no_layout_in_the_fold exactly, requires no wireframe rendering at all (just the box table), and closes most of the gap the fold's blindness leaves. It should be run at capture time and its result stored as a per-address flag, so that the fold can carry a 'not rendered' marker without ever having read geometry itself -- the flag is data keyed by address, exactly like any other peripheral value. Two cautions. The check is not free of adversarial response: an attacker can render an injection at full size in a colour matching the background, or behind an opaque element, or with clip-path, none of which a bounding box detects -- so the box check catches the common cases and not the careful ones, and the residual must be declared. And the wireframe itself preserves whatever labels it draws, so injected text placed in a visible element appears in the wireframe like any other text.
provenance_carrying: None natively -- a grid of characters carries no origin, address or time. As argued above, addresses must be attached explicitly, either inline per box or via a legend. Once attached, the wireframe inherits the trie's full provenance because it is keyed on the same addresses; without attachment it carries nothing and cannot be audited. The geometry table that underlies it is naturally address-keyed and therefore provenance-carrying by construction, which is another reason to treat the table as the artifact and the grid as a rendering.
roundtrip_safety: Lossy and not a fixed point -- a wireframe cannot be parsed back into geometry. A weaker and useful invariant exists: rendering the same geometry at the same resolution twice must produce identical output, and rendering at a finer resolution must not CONTRADICT a coarser one (relations asserted at low resolution should still hold at high resolution, even if new relations become visible). That monotonic-refinement property is checkable, is the spatial analogue of the budget-monotonicity check in item 29, and would catch quantisation bugs. Escaping matters here in an unusual way: page text drawn into cells can contain box-drawing characters, pipes, dashes or newlines that corrupt the grid, so cell content must be sanitised of grid-structural characters before placement -- an injection vector that is specific to this representation and that the literature does not mention.
token_budget_and_ordering: Governed by the quadratic cost above and by the read/write asymmetry. BUDGET: an 80x24 grid is roughly 2,000 characters of structure before content, which against a small model's practical per-emission budget (on the order of 1,500 tokens per item 30's analysis) means a wireframe is a whole-budget artifact. It therefore must be an explicitly requested actuator-layer operation, never part of a default read, and its resolution should be the coarsest that answers the question at hand. ORDERING: a grid is a two-dimensional object flattened into a one-dimensional token sequence, so it has an implicit reading order that the model must reconstruct, and it is highly repetitive in a way that is exactly the distractor profile item 30 identifies as harmful. That argues for placing a wireframe LATE in the context (where attention is favoured past 50% fill) and for keeping it small, and against emitting one alongside a large content payload. READ/WRITE ASYMMETRY IS THE KEY DESIGN FACT: models interpret ASCII layouts substantially better than they construct them, with a 13-27 percentage point gap and GPT-4.1 at 72.5% interpreting versus 53.6% constructing. The project's design has the model READING a wireframe the sensor produced, which is the favourable direction -- this is real evidential support for the approach. The corollary is a prohibition: never ask the model to produce, edit or transform a wireframe, because that is the direction where it fails roughly half the time and the errors propagate silently into downstream answers. Any spatial ACTION should be expressed as an address plus a verb, not as a modification to a grid.
representation_cost: Quadratic in linear resolution: an 80x24 grid is about 1,920 cells, a 120x40 grid about 4,800, a 200x60 grid about 12,000, before accounting for tokenisation of whitespace runs (which varies by tokeniser and can be better or worse than one token per character). What is bought per token is coarse spatial relation and nothing else -- no content beyond short labels, no state beyond glyph conventions, no structure beyond adjacency and containment. Compared with the alternatives it is far cheaper than a screenshot (tens of thousands of image tokens) and far more expensive than a prose statement of the few spatial facts that usually matter, which is the comparison most often skipped: 'the login form is in a modal covering the page centre' is fifteen tokens and answers the question a 2,000-token wireframe was drawn to answer. A targeted spatial-query interface -- ask whether A is above B, or which elements are in the viewport -- would dominate a rendered grid on cost for most questions, and only wholesale layout comprehension justifies the grid.
what_could_be_adopted: Six things. (1) THE GEOMETRY-AS-ADDRESS-KEYED-SIDE-TABLE architecture, which the project already specifies and which this item confirms: store four numbers plus a visibility flag per address, treat every rendering as derived, and never maintain the rendering incrementally. (2) THE CONCEALMENT CHECK described under adversarial_exposure -- compare fold addresses against addresses with a non-degenerate rendered box and flag the difference as a per-address marker. This is the single most valuable idea in this item: it lets a layout-blind fold carry a rendering-derived concealment flag without ever reading layout itself, addressing most of the rendering-based concealment class while keeping the constraint intact. (3) THE READ-DON'T-WRITE RULE, backed by the 13-27 point construction gap: emit wireframes for the model to read, never ask it to produce or modify one. (4) DISPLAY-WIDTH-CORRECT CELL COMPUTATION (East Asian Width tables, zero-width combining marks) and an explicit, documented policy for RTL labels -- without which the wireframe is silently wrong for a large fraction of the world's content. (5) DECLARED-LOSS HEADERS on every rendering: downscale factor, cell size, overlap count, fraction of document outside the rendered region, truncation markers. (6) A TARGETED SPATIAL-QUERY INTERFACE as the default and the full grid as the exception, since most spatial questions are answerable in a few tokens from the box table directly and the grid's quadratic cost is rarely justified. Explicitly NOT to be adopted: routine wireframe emission alongside content; any attempt to maintain a wireframe incrementally; and reliance on the wireframe as a content or state record rather than as a locator.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS with one boundary to hold. Rendering boxes from geometry names no region and classifies nothing -- a box is a box. The violation would occur if the renderer began labelling regions by inferred role (drawing a 'nav bar' or a 'sidebar'), or if wireframe generation were conditioned on an inferred page archetype; conditioning on mechanical signals (column count, sibling box-size variance) or on explicit request stays clean. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY, unambiguously and by definition -- this is a geometry-consuming representation and there is no layout-free version of it. The project's existing placement of the ASCII wireframe on the actuator side is exactly right and this item supplies the reasons: it forces layout (a cost and a faint detectability signal the fold does not have), it is quadratic in resolution, it cannot be maintained incrementally, and it is pinned to a browser/OS/font/viewport tuple. IMPORTANT REFINEMENT: the derived per-address 'not rendered' FLAG produced by the concealment check is NOT layout in the fold -- it is a peripheral value keyed by address, computed on the actuator side and read like any other, which is precisely the arrangement the constraint permits. That distinction is what makes the safety benefit available without breaching the constraint, and it should be stated explicitly in the design rather than left implicit. o_delta: REJECTED FOR INCREMENTAL MAINTENANCE. Layout is global, so one DOM change can move every box; CSS-driven layout change produces a wholly different wireframe with an empty mutation record; scroll, font loading and media loading all reflow with no DOM signal. There is no bounded per-change cost and there cannot be. The correct posture is on-demand regeneration, and any O(delta) claim must exclude the geometry peripheral by name. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- geometry comes from a real rendered page and there is nothing to stub. The measured claims from this literature are NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY for web layout: Text2Space is synthetic spatial graphs, ASCIIBench is ASCII art, and no benchmark uses a rendered browser viewport, so the read/write asymmetry transfers as a direction and not as a rate. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NO CONFLICT, and worth noting as a mild ADVANTAGE -- geometry is computed over the composed tree including closed roots, so a box exists for content the DOM will not hand over; this is not a bypass (the box carries no content, only extent) and it means the concealment check can flag the PRESENCE of unreachable rendered content, which is a legitimate and useful declaration. OVERALL VERDICT: actuator-layer only, adopt the geometry side table and the concealment check, obey the read-don't-write rule, fix display width and RTL before trusting any output, and exclude the whole representation from the delta guarantee explicitly.
governance_signal_handling: None; no retrieval is involved. One tangential point: rendering requires the page to have loaded its resources (fonts, images, stylesheets), so a wireframe implicitly attests that those third-party fetches occurred -- which is a governance-relevant fact about what was retrieved, and one that is invisible in a DOM-only capture. If per-origin governance matters, the network log rather than the wireframe is the place to record it.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: A wireframe is a coarse image of what was on screen and should be classified with screenshots rather than with serialisations: on an authenticated page it discloses the arrangement and any labels drawn into cells, including personal data appearing in visible text. It is far lower resolution than a screenshot and therefore substantially less exposing -- a genuine minimisation advantage if a visual record is needed at all, and worth preferring over a screenshot wherever a coarse visual witness suffices (gate-state recording, for instance). The underlying geometry table is non-content -- four numbers per address -- and carries essentially no personal data on its own, which makes it the right thing to retain persistently while treating rendered grids as ephemeral derivations. Erasure follows the address scheme. [uncertain] on the specific analysis under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, which is item 19's subject.
